```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
```


## Q1 Birthday Simulation
```{r}
# Randomly sample n birthdays from 1–365. If the number of unique birthdays is less than n, then True at least two people share the same birthday; if false, unique birthdays number should = n.

birthday_sim = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)

  n_unique = length(unique(birthdays))

  same_birthday = n_unique < n

  same_birthday
}
# Test
birthday_sim(2)

birthday_sim(10)

birthday_sim(50)

birthday_sim(365)
```

```{r}
# 10,000 times simulations
birthday_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  )

birthday_df

birthday_results =
  birthday_df |>
  mutate(
    same_birthday = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_sim)
  )

birthday_results

# Probability
birthday_stat =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    probability = mean(same_birthday)
  )

birthday_stat |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "seagreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Shared Birthdays by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  )
```
The probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases with group size. This result makes sense because larger groups contain more people, increasing the chance of shared birthdays. The probability approaches 1 but does not reach 1 within the simulated group sizes, since there is still a small chance that everyone has a different birthday.


## Q2 Longitudinal Study
```{r}
# List files
participant =
  tibble(files = list.files("data/data/"))

participant =
  participant |>
  mutate(
    path = str_c("data/data/", files))

participant

# Read files and save as new variable
participant =
  participant |>
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)
  )

participant
```

```{r}
# Tidy-up: Unnest → Extract group → Reshape weekly data (wide to long) → Finalize
participant_tidy =
  participant |>
  unnest(data)

participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  mutate(
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    subj = str_sub(files, 1, 6))

participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  mutate(
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3))

participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  )

participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  select(
    group,
    subj = files,
    week,
    outcome)

participant_tidy

# Subject ID revision
participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  mutate(
    subj = str_replace(subj, ".csv", ""))

participant_tidy
```

```{r}
# Plot
participant_tidy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome,
             group = subj, color = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~group) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Outcomes by Study Group",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome")

# No noticeable difference in the plot whether week treated as character or numeric, but technically it should be numerical to represents time
participant_tidy =
  participant_tidy |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week)
  )

participant_tidy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome,
             group = subj, color = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~group) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Outcomes by Study Group",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome")
```
The control group shows fluctuations in outcome over time around approximately 1.25, while the experimental group shows a generally increasing trend across the eight weeks with higher outcome values toward the end of the study.

## Q3 True Effect Simulation
```{r}
# Set
n = 30
sigma = 5
mu = 0

# One-sample test simulation
sim_ttest = function(mu) {

  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )

  test_result = t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0)

  test_tidy = broom::tidy(test_result)

  test_tidy = test_tidy |>
    select(estimate, p.value)

  test_tidy
}

# 5,000 times simulation
sim_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  )

sim_results =
  sim_df |>
  mutate(
    result = map(true_mu, sim_ttest))

sim_results
```

```{r}
# Statistical power plot
sim_results |>
  unnest(result) |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(p.value < 0.05)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Proportion of Rejected Null Hypotheses"
  )
```
Statistical power increases as the true mean increases, which makes sense because larger effects are easier to detect. When the true mean is 0, the rejection proportion is around 0.05, which is consistent with the significance level.

```{r}
# Average estimate plot
sim_results |>
  unnest(result) |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    avg_estimate = mean(estimate)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_estimate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean"
  )
```
The average estimated mean is almost identical to the true mean and shows a perfectly straight line. This looks a bit suspicious to me, but it should make sense since it's an unbiased estimator of the population mean, and most of the random differences get cancelled.

```{r}
# Rejected tests average estimate plot
sim_results |>
  unnest(result) |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    avg_estimate = mean(estimate)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_estimate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean Among Rejected Tests",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean"
  )
```
When the true mean is small, the average estimated mean is higher than the actual value. But the average estimate is gonna get closer and closer to the true mean as the true mean increases. This may be because when the true mean is small, only estimates that are far enough from 0 are likely to have a p-value below 0.05, in another word, more extreme results, which makes the average higher. As the true mean increases, more tests reject the null hypothesis, so the difference becomes smaller.
